dialogue:
JAMIE: A purchase request goes into an approval chain and disappears. Not rejected. Not approved. Just haunting a spreadsheet. That is our imaginary office today, and I want to give its ghost a forwarding address.
RUFUS: Finally. Digital transformation for the recently departed invoice.
ALEX: Hold on. Who actually gets their afternoon back?
JAMIE: In the example we're designing, the person chasing missing information. SAP's October twenty-seventh TechEd announcement describes n8n workflows inside Joule Studio for early adopters, with broader availability to follow. That's the verified capability. This missing-approval scenario is our hypothetical application, not a customer success story.
RUFUS: Early adopters. A velvet rope outside the stationery cupboard.
JAMIE: You mock the cupboard until nobody approves your replacement microphone.
ALEX: She has identified our single point of failure.
JAMIE: Here's the idea. A request arrives. A proposed workflow gathers its details, flags missing information and prepares a summary for a person to review. It does not approve the spending. We decide where the human must step in before anything moves.
RUFUS: I'm with you on that separation. Collecting paperwork and authorising money should not quietly become the same job.
ALEX: But isn't this a very expensive way to say, fill in the form properly?
JAMIE: Sometimes, yes! That's the useful challenge. If a clearer form solves it, fix the form. I wouldn't buy an agent to admire it wearing a tiny procurement badge.
RUFUS: Shame. I had already selected its cufflinks.
JAMIE: But when information arrives through several handoffs, I'd test whether a draft summary makes the missing piece easier to spot. Test it. Don't announce savings before anyone has measured them.
ALEX: What can someone actually try without access to SAP's early-adopter program?
JAMIE: Take one fictional purchase request. Map three handoffs on paper. At each stop, write what the next person needs and who can authorise it. Then see whether a simple checklist fixes the confusion before designing an AI workflow. No real customer information needed.
RUFUS: So your exciting AI discovery ends with permission to buy less AI.
JAMIE: Absolutely. My segment, my standards. Useful beats shiny.
ALEX: And if we test a workflow later, compare missing-information errors and handoff time against that checklist.
JAMIE: Exactly. Find the gap, keep the person in charge, measure whether it helps. The ghost does not get purchasing authority.
review_note: Producer draft; full production factual audit remains required. SAP capability and early-adopter limits are sourced in the case; workflow is explicitly hypothetical.
